answer.rationale: Constraints dominate here: the primary contract lapses in 14 days, the line is at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, and I get exactly one move. That combination makes switch_primary_vendor the worst-timed option regardless of how attractive memory_c2's cost result looks \u2014 a migration inside 14 days at zero slack converts a cost problem into a delivery failure, and the mandate says reduce TCO WITHOUT increasing delivery risk. defer_decision (memory_c5) is inapplicable: c5 concerned a non-critical service that continued month-to-month, whereas this contract does not auto-renew, so deferring means an actual supply gap. add_second_source (memory_c3) is genuinely valuable but does not answer the expiring primary agreement, so it cannot be the single move this cycle. Plain renew_incumbent (memory_c1) protects delivery but concedes the entire 18% target. That leaves negotiate_terms \u2014 with an important reframing: the incumbent refused to reopen PRICE this cycle, which is a different lever than the one memory_c6 describes. c6 says a multi-year commitment unlocked volume pricing without narrowing scope; term length, volume tiering, and payment terms (memory_c4's second lever) are still open even when in-cycle price is closed. So I intend to trade tenor and volume commitment for unit cost, structured as a guarded step: a short bridge/renewal that secures continuity past the 14-day cliff plus a multi-year option contingent on verified pricing, rather than an immediate long lock-in. I am verifying memory_c6 to confirm the volume-pricing discount was real, scope-preserving, and on a comparable component rather than a one-off, since my whole plan rests on it; and memory_c2 to learn the conditions of that low-cost switch \u2014 if it was a low-criticality part at slack capacity with a long onboarding runway, it is not evidence for switching a constrained primary at 94% utilization, and it also tells me whether that vendor is a credible qualification target for a second source next cycle. Two honest risks I am not papering over: a multi-year commitment buys unit cost by spending future flexibility and deepens single-source exposure, which is precisely the failure mode memory_c3 was written to prevent; and 18% may simply not be reachable through terms alone. If verification shows c6's discount was narrow or conditional, I expect to fall back to a bridge renewal plus dual-sourcing at the next review and report a partial gap against the mandate rather than force the number by taking on delivery risk. I will not let the spend target rewrite the risk constraint.
